subject: Cooking
title: Beer's 10,000-Year Journey
description: A micro-lesson that makes Beer's 10,000-Year Journey usable.

hook.text: Some archaeologists believe humans settled down to farm grain not for bread — but for beer.

buildup.text: The earliest evidence of beer dates to 11,000 BCE in Göbekli Tepe, Turkey — before agriculture itself.

discovery.text: Ancient beer was thick, nutritious, and low-alcohol. Workers, soldiers, and children all drank it safely.

twist.text: The German Reinheitsgebot of 1516 restricted beer to just water, barley, and hops — still law today.

climax.text: Craft brewing has revived ancient techniques — sour ales, wild yeasts, and fruit additions are 'new' but ancient.

punchline.text: Beer might be the reason civilization exists.

quiz.question: What is the Reinheitsgebot?
options: A German beer purity law from 1516

details.summary: Beer production dates back at least 10,000 years to early Neolithic settlements. Ancient Sumerians, Egyptians, and Chinese all independently developed brewing techniques. Some archaeologists believe the desire to brew beer actually motivated the agricultural revolution.
details.whyItMatters: Beer is one of civilization's oldest fermented beverages. The theory that beer drove the invention of agriculture reframes fermentation as a force that shaped human history.
takeaways: The oldest evidence of beer dates to around 10,000 BCE in China
Sumerians had a goddess of brewing named Ninkasi
The beer-before-bread hypothesis suggests beer drove agriculture

faq.question: Did beer really come before bread?
faq.answer: Some archaeologists argue that fermenting grain into beer provided more nutritional value than eating raw grain, motivating early humans to cultivate crops. The evidence is debated, but beer and bread likely co-evolved since both require harvested grain and similar processing.

faq.question: What was ancient beer like?
faq.answer: Ancient beer was thick, cloudy, and often drunk through straws to filter sediment. It was lower in alcohol and sometimes flavored with dates, honey, or herbs instead of hops. Egyptian workers received beer as daily wages, and Sumerian taverns were common social venues.
